identity.title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking Autonomous Exploitation of Adversarial Example Defenses

problem.claim: Assess whether LLMs can autonomously exploit defenses against adversarial examples.

gap.claim: Existing security benchmarks often proxy real-world tasks rather than directly measuring success on tasks regularly performed by machine-learning security experts.

contributions.claim: Introduces AutoAdvExBench for evaluating autonomous LLM exploitation of adversarial-example defenses.
Releases the benchmark publicly through a GitHub repository.

stated_novelty.claim: The benchmark directly measures LLM success on expert-relevant adversarial-machine-learning tasks, unlike proxy-based security benchmarks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The strongest reported agent ensemble breaks 87% of CTF-like defenses but 37% of real-world defenses.
For CTF-like defenses, Sonnet 3.5 and Opus 4 achieve 75% and 79% attack success, respectively; on real-world defenses, the rates are 13% and 30%.

narrative_sequence.summary: The authors introduce a benchmark for autonomous LLM exploitation of adversarial-example defenses.
They position it as a direct measure of expert-relevant task success rather than a proxy benchmark.
Their strongest ensemble performs much better on CTF-like defenses than on real-world defenses, revealing a large reported difficulty gap.
Sonnet 3.5 and Opus 4 have similar reported attack success on CTF-like defenses (75% and 79%), but a wider separation on real-world defenses (13% and 30%).
The benchmark is made available via GitHub.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates CTF-like from real-world defenses and reports both aggregate and model-specific success rates.

lessons.interpretation: Benchmark conclusions become more informative when evaluation tracks task realism and reports whether proxy performance transfers.
lessons.application: When presenting a benchmark, define realism-based subsets and compare rankings or success rates across them.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the deployment setting is intentionally limited to synthetic or educational tasks.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the number or composition of defenses, attack protocols, agent configurations, or evaluation criteria.
It does not report uncertainty, statistical tests, or whether the benchmark’s real-world subset represents the broader ecosystem.

editorial_revisions.before: They report that CTF performance does not consistently predict real-world-defense performance across Sonnet 3.5 and Opus 4.
editorial_revisions.after: Sonnet 3.5 and Opus 4 have similar reported attack success on CTF-like defenses (75% and 79%), but a wider separation on real-world defenses (13% and 30%).
